cues.text: Welcome to Solutions.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Most concentration errors begin with the denominator.
Molarity is moles of solute divided by litres of final solution.
Molality is moles of solute divided by kilograms of solvent.
The words solution and solvent are not interchangeable.
Suppose twenty grams of solute are dissolved in one hundred eighty grams of
solvent.
The final solution mass is two hundred grams, so the mass percentage is ten
percent.
If the solute molar mass is one hundred grams per mole, the solute amount is
zero point two zero zero moles.
Divide by zero point one eight zero kilograms of solvent to obtain molality
about one point one one moles per kilogram.
We cannot calculate molarity until the final solution volume or enough
information to infer it is supplied.
Do not use solvent volume as solution volume or assume volumes always add
exactly.
If the solution density were one point two zero grams per millilitre, its two
hundred gram mass would occupy about one hundred sixty six point seven
millilitres.
The molarity would then be one point two zero moles per litre.
At fixed composition, molality does not change when thermal expansion changes
the volume.
Molarity generally does.
Mole fraction is the moles of a component divided by total moles of all
components; all mole fractions sum to one.
One mole of A and three moles of B give mole fractions one quarter and three
quarters.
Volume percentage uses solute volume divided by final solution volume under a
stated convention and temperature.
Before using any concentration, write down its numerator and denominator.
That small step prevents confusing mass percentage with mole fraction or
molarity with molality.
For an ideal liquid solution, Raoult's law says that each volatile component
contributes a partial vapour pressure equal to its liquid mole fraction times
the vapour pressure of the pure component at the same temperature.
Add these partial pressures to obtain the total.
Consider an equimolar ideal mixture of A and B.
Their pure vapour pressures are eighty and forty kilopascals.
A contributes one half of eighty, or forty kilopascals.
B contributes one half of forty, or twenty.
The total is sixty kilopascals.
Assuming an ideal vapour, A's mole fraction in that vapour is its partial
pressure divided by total pressure: forty over sixty, or two thirds.
The liquid was one half A, while the vapour is richer in the more volatile
component A.
Keep liquid mole fraction x separate from vapour mole fraction y.
For a nonvolatile solute, only the solvent contributes appreciably.
If solvent mole fraction is zero point nine zero and pure solvent vapour
pressure is one hundred kilopascals, the solution pressure is ninety
kilopascals.
In the ideal solution model with one nonvolatile solute, relative vapour
pressure lowering equals the solute mole fraction.
Dissociation or association requires consistent counting of the species
present.
Ideal mixing has zero enthalpy change and zero volume change of mixing.
Positive deviations from Raoult's law give a higher vapour pressure than the
ideal prediction, commonly associated with weaker unlike interactions.
Negative deviations give a lower pressure, commonly associated with stronger
unlike interactions.
Sufficiently strong deviations can produce azeotropes, where liquid and vapour
compositions coincide during boiling at the specified pressure.
Do not infer an azeotrope from every small deviation.
Detailed phase diagrams require additional treatment.
Always compare pure vapour pressures at the same temperature.
Colligative properties in the dilute solution model depend on the number of
dissolved particles rather than their chemical identity.
Boiling point elevation equals the van't Hoff factor i times the solvent's
boiling constant times molality.
Freezing point depression equals i times the solvent's freezing constant times
molality.
The freezing depression is a positive magnitude; subtract it from the pure
solvent freezing point.
These relations apply approximately to dilute solutions with suitable
nonvolatile solutes and the usual solvent phase assumptions.
Consider zero point zero one zero zero moles of a non electrolyte dissolved in
zero point one zero zero kilograms of water.
Molality is zero point one zero zero moles per kilogram.
Taking i as one and the freezing constant as one point eight six kelvin
kilograms per mole, the freezing depression is zero point one eight six
kelvin.
If pure water freezes at zero degrees Celsius under the stated conditions,
this
solution freezes at minus zero point one eight six degrees Celsius.
A temperature difference of one kelvin equals a difference of one degree
Celsius.
For a second example, ten grams of a non electrolyte with molar mass one
hundred eighty grams per mole are dissolved in one hundred grams of water.
First convert the solute mass into zero point zero five five six moles.
Divide by zero point one zero zero kilograms of solvent to get molality about
zero point five five six.
The predicted depression is about one point zero three kelvin for i equal to
one.
The one hundred ten gram solution mass does not belong in the molality
denominator.
If the effective particle factor doubles at the same formal molality, the
dilute model predicts twice the temperature shift.
The constants belong to the solvent, and the particle factor describes how the
dissolved solute behaves.
A semipermeable membrane allows the solvent to pass while retaining the chosen
solute.
Solvent tends to move toward the solution with lower solvent chemical
potential.
Osmotic pressure is the excess pressure required to stop this net solvent flow
under the specified conditions.
For an ideal dilute solution, osmotic pressure equals i times the formal
solute
molarity times R times absolute temperature.
Formal molarity counts the solute amount before applying the particle factor.
Suppose a non electrolyte solution has concentration zero point one zero zero
moles per litre at three hundred kelvin.
Use R equal to zero point zero eight two zero five seven litre atmospheres per
mole kelvin.
Multiplying gives osmotic pressure about two point four six atmospheres.
Pressure is not measured in kelvin, and temperature must not be inserted in
degrees Celsius.
Now infer a molar mass.
Two point zero zero grams of a non electrolyte are made up to one point zero
zero litre of solution.
At three hundred kelvin, the osmotic pressure is zero point two four six
atmospheres.
Replace molarity by mass divided by molar mass and solution volume.
Rearranging gives molar mass equals i times mass times R times temperature,
divided by osmotic pressure times volume.
With i equal to one, the result is about two hundred grams per mole.
Check the units: litre atmospheres cancel with pressure times volume, leaving
grams per mole.
This sensitivity to low concentrations makes osmotic pressure useful for large
molecules, provided the membrane and dilute solution assumptions hold.
Equal osmotic pressures at the same temperature require equal effective
particle concentrations.
Equal formal molarities alone are insufficient if particle factors differ.
In every osmotic pressure calculation, use final solution volume, the
compatible gas constant and the correct particle factor.
The van't Hoff factor compares the effective number of solute particles with
the number expected from the formula amount added.
In a simple ideal dissociation model, suppose a fraction alpha dissociates and
each dissociated formula unit produces nu particles.
Starting with one mole of formula units, one minus alpha remains intact and nu
times alpha appears as products.
The total particle count is one plus alpha times nu minus one.
If eighty percent dissociates into two particles, i is one point eight zero.
Complete ideal dissociation of sodium chloride would give two, although
measured values can differ because real solutions are not perfectly ideal.
Association reduces the particle count.
If a fraction alpha of initial molecules combines into groups of n, the
remaining monomers contribute one minus alpha, and the groups contribute alpha
divided by n.
Thus i equals one minus alpha times one minus one over n.
Imagine one hundred initial molecules with half of them forming dimers.
Fifty molecules stay single.
The other fifty make twenty five dimers.
There are seventy five particles in total, so i is zero point seven five.
Do not count each dimer as two independent dissolved particles.
If a colligative measurement is analysed while incorrectly assuming i equals
one, the apparent molar mass equals the true molar mass divided by the actual
particle factor.
Association therefore makes the apparent molar mass larger.
A true molar mass of one hundred eighty with i zero point seven five appears
as
two hundred forty grams per mole.
Dissociation has the opposite effect.
This simple degree model assumes one specified association or dissociation
process and neglects additional nonideal interactions.
Finish by checking the denominator, solvent constants, temperature scale and
effective particle number.
The companion notes include three worked examples and six original questions.
This Unit five foundation is followed by further phase diagram, azeotrope and
mixed problem practice.
Density connects solution volume to the masses needed for molality.
Take a one point zero zero molar solution of a solute with molar mass sixty
grams per mole and solution density one point zero four grams per millilitre
at
the stated temperature.
Choose one litre of solution.
It contains one mole, or sixty grams, of solute.
Its total mass is one thousand forty grams.
Subtracting the solute leaves nine hundred eighty grams of solvent, or zero
point nine eight zero kilogram.
Molality is therefore one divided by zero point nine eight zero, about one
point zero two moles per kilogram.
Do not divide by the total solution mass.
In the general conversion formula, density in grams per millilitre makes one
litre weigh one thousand times density in grams.
Subtract molarity times solute molar mass, then convert the remaining grams to
kilograms.
This calculation assumes a single identified solute and a correctly specified
final solution density.
Molarity and density must refer to the same temperature.
A negative calculated solvent mass signals inconsistent data or a unit error.
Henry law describes dilute dissolved gas in equilibrium with its gas phase at
a
specified temperature.
Several conventions use the same name, so write the equation before
interpreting its constant.
Here the gas partial pressure equals K H times its dissolved mole fraction.
Suppose K H is forty thousand bar and the relevant gas partial pressure is two
bar.
The dissolved mole fraction is two divided by forty thousand, or five times
ten
to the minus five.
Use the gas partial pressure rather than the total pressure of an unrelated
gas
mixture.
In this convention, a larger K H means a smaller dissolved mole fraction at
the
same pressure.
A constant defined by concentration divided by pressure has the opposite
interpretation.
Temperature changes the constant; do not compare values at different
temperatures as if conditions were identical.
The simple relationship assumes a dilute solution and no major chemical
reaction changing the gas species in solution.
Increasing pressure increases equilibrium solubility within the model, but
equilibrium solubility does not specify how fast the gas enters the liquid.
Keep the pressure unit consistent.
For an ideal liquid mixture, each component follows the partial pressure
prediction from its liquid mole fraction and pure liquid vapour pressure.
Real mixtures can lie above or below that prediction.
In a common positive deviation picture, unlike molecule attractions are less
favourable than the corresponding like molecule interactions, and total vapour
pressure is higher than the ideal prediction.
Negative deviation gives lower vapour pressure.
Mixing enthalpy and volume can provide supporting evidence, but they require
actual mixture data.
A sufficiently large deviation can produce an azeotrope at a specified
pressure.
At that composition, the equilibrium vapour and liquid have the same
composition, so ordinary fractional distillation cannot carry that mixture
past
the azeotropic composition.
Minimum boiling azeotropes are associated with a suitable positive deviation;
maximum boiling ones with a suitable negative deviation.
Not every nonideal mixture forms an azeotrope.
Nor does an azeotrope require equal mole fractions of the two components.
State whether a graph holds pressure or temperature fixed before reading its
boiling or vapour pressure extrema.
Boiling elevation can provide a molar mass when the solvent amount and
particle
behaviour are known.
Dissolve one point eight zero grams of a nonvolatile non electrolyte in one
hundred grams of solvent.
Let the solvent boiling constant be zero point five two kelvin kilograms per
mole, and the measured elevation be zero point zero five two kelvin.
Assume a dilute solution and particle factor one.
Dividing the elevation by the boiling constant gives molality zero point one
zero zero moles per kilogram.
Multiply by zero point one zero zero kilogram of solvent to obtain zero point
zero one zero zero moles of solute.
Divide one point eight zero grams by that amount to get one hundred eighty
grams per mole.
The measured elevation is a positive difference, not the absolute boiling
temperature.
If the pure solvent boils at one hundred degrees Celsius under the stated
pressure, the model solution boils at one hundred point zero five two degrees
Celsius.
Association or dissociation changes the effective particle count and therefore
the inferred molar mass.
Check the assumed particle factor and solvent mass before treating a numerical
answer as a molecular formula.
Consider a solute that produces three ions per formula unit in the ideal
dissociation model.
Starting with one mole of formula units, a fraction alpha dissociates.
One minus alpha mole remains intact and three alpha moles appear as ions.
Total particles are one plus two alpha.
If a dilute colligative measurement gives particle factor two point six zero,
alpha is zero point eight zero, or eighty percent.
The complete dissociation limit is three, so a value above three would not fit
this simple single process model.
Real electrolyte interactions can also affect measured factors.
Now compare osmotic pressures at the same temperature.
A zero point one zero zero molar non electrolyte has effective particle
concentration zero point one zero zero molar.
A salt solution with factor two point six zero matches it at formal
concentration zero point one zero zero divided by two point six zero, about
zero point zero three eight five molar.
Equal formal molarities would not be isotonic here.
These equations assume the stated membranes retain the relevant solutes and
that the dilute solution model is adequate.
For an ideal binary solution with a nonvolatile solute, the solvent vapour
pressure equals solvent mole fraction times pure solvent vapour pressure.
Take one point zero zero mole solvent and zero point one zero zero mole
solute,
with pure solvent pressure twenty seven point zero kilopascals.
The solvent mole fraction is one divided by one point one, or about zero point
nine zero nine one.
Solution vapour pressure is therefore about twenty four point five five
kilopascals.
The relative lowering is one minus the solvent mole fraction, equal to solute
mole fraction zero point zero nine zero nine one.
Replacing the total mole denominator by the solvent amount alone would give
zero point one zero zero; that is a dilute approximation rather than the exact
binary mole fraction.
The difference is already visible at the supplied composition.
This model assumes the solute contributes negligible vapour and the solvent
follows ideal behaviour.
A volatile second component requires its own partial pressure, and an
electrolyte or associating solute can require additional particle and activity
treatment.
State the species counted and the ideality assumptions before converting a
measured pressure lowering into a molar mass or composition.
A colligative effect depends on the combined effective particle amount when
several solutes share the same solvent.
Consider zero point zero one zero zero mole glucose and zero point zero two
zero zero mole sodium chloride in zero point one zero zero kilogram water.
Assume a dilute ideal comparison, negligible solute interactions and complete
sodium chloride dissociation into two ions.
Glucose contributes zero point zero one zero zero mole particles, while the
salt contributes zero point zero four zero zero.
Total effective particle amount is zero point zero five zero zero mole.
Dividing by the common solvent mass gives zero point five zero zero mole
particles per kilogram.
With the supplied freezing point constant one point eight six kelvin kilogram
per mole, the depression is zero point nine three zero kelvin.
Do not give each solute a separate full solvent mass and then add solvent
amounts, or treat the electrolyte as one undissociated particle under the
stated assumption.
In an actual electrolyte solution, an effective factor can differ from the
integer ion count because of nonideal interactions.
The calculation is an ideal particle accounting exercise, not a guarantee of
exact experimental freezing temperature for an arbitrary concentrated mixture.
Association reduces the number of independently moving solute particles
without
removing the mass of the original material.
Consider an elementary dimerization model in which two monomers join to form
one dimer.
If a fraction alpha of the original monomer units associates, starting from
one
mole of monomer units leaves one minus alpha mole monomers and alpha divided
by
two mole dimers.
The total particle amount is one minus alpha divided by two, which gives the
ideal particle factor.
Suppose true monomer molar mass is sixty and a suitable colligative
calculation, made while ignoring association, reports apparent molar mass
eighty grams per mole.
The particle factor is sixty divided by eighty, or zero point seven five.
Solving gives alpha one half.
Thus half the original monomer units are incorporated into dimers.
From one initial mole of units, there are zero point five zero mole free
monomers and zero point two five zero mole dimers, or zero point seven five
zero mole particles.
Apparent molar mass eighty is not a new molecular formula mass of a pure
dimer.
The inference assumes only this association process and a suitable dilute
ideal
colligative model.
A membrane that passes solvent but excludes the stated solutes can separate
osmotic and applied pressure effects.
Compare ideal dilute non electrolyte solutions at three hundred kelvin with
particle concentrations zero point one zero zero and zero point two zero zero
molar.
With equal initial hydrostatic pressure, solvent tends toward the more
concentrated side.
The opposing osmotic pressure difference is R T times the concentration
difference.
Using R zero point zero eight two zero five seven litre atmosphere per mole
kelvin gives about two point four six atmospheres.
Applying that pressure difference to the concentrated side can balance the
ideal osmotic tendency.
A larger applied difference, such as three point zero zero atmospheres in this
model, can drive solvent in the reverse direction toward the dilute side.
This is the thermodynamic comparison underlying reverse osmosis, not a
prediction of a particular membrane's flow rate.
Real membranes, concentration polarization, solute passage and solution
nonideality affect performance.
The relevant threshold here is the pressure difference between the two
specified solutions, rather than the concentrated solution's osmotic pressure
relative to pure solvent.
Keep the applied side and the direction of each driving effect explicit.
Deviation from an ideal vapour pressure prediction can be identified from a
defined comparison, but an azeotrope requires additional evidence.
Suppose a binary liquid at fixed temperature has equal liquid mole fractions
and pure component vapour pressures eighty and forty kilopascals.
Raoult's ideal total pressure prediction is one half times eighty plus one
half
times forty, giving sixty kilopascals.
If the measured total is seventy five at the same temperature and composition,
that point lies above the ideal reference and shows positive total pressure
deviation.
It does not by itself prove that an azeotrope exists.
At an azeotropic composition, equilibrium vapour and liquid compositions match
under the specified conditions.
A full composition dependent dataset or suitable boiling behaviour is needed
to
establish that special point.
Likewise positive deviation does not force an azeotrope at equal mole
fractions, and not every nonideal mixture has one.
Use mixing enthalpy, volume and interaction information only when actually
supplied rather than inventing them from one pressure value.
This is a data interpretation method: match temperature, liquid composition
and
reference definitions before deciding which claim the evidence supports.
A crystalline hydrate contains water that can become part of the solvent after
complete dissolution.
Consider a supplied ideal model: two hundred fifty grams of a hydrate with
molar mass two hundred fifty grams per mole contains five waters of
crystallization per formula unit.
Each water has molar mass eighteen.
The sample therefore contains one mole of anhydrous salt formula units and
ninety grams hydration water.
Dissolve it in nine hundred ten grams added water.
The final solvent water mass is one thousand grams, so the formal salt
molality
is one point zero zero mole per kilogram.
Dividing by the added water alone would give an incorrect denominator for this
model.
If that salt then dissociates ideally into two ions per formula unit, the
ideal
solute particle molality is two point zero zero moles per kilogram.
Do not count hydration water as extra solute particles after it has joined the
solvent.
This is a stated complete dissolution model without hydrolysis, retained bound
complexes or other reactions; actual hydration and activities may require a
more detailed description.
Concentration conversions can be reversed to infer a solution density when
consistent data are supplied.
Suppose a solution has molarity two point zero zero moles per litre and
molality two point five zero moles per kilogram, for a solute with molar mass
sixty point zero grams per mole.
Choose one litre of solution.
It contains two moles solute with mass one hundred twenty grams.
Molality gives solvent mass two divided by two point five zero, or zero point
eight zero zero kilogram.
Total solution mass is therefore nine hundred twenty grams in one thousand
millilitres, giving density zero point nine two zero gram per millilitre.
The two concentrations refer to the same sample and temperature.
Molarity uses solution volume, while molality uses solvent mass, so they
cannot
be equated just because both count moles.
The inferred density is a consistency result for supplied data, not a
universal
density for that solute.
Temperature can change volume and molarity even when composition and molality
remain unchanged in a closed sample.
Two colligative measurements on the same solution can check whether a single
ideal particle count model is internally consistent.
Use a supplied solvent with boiling elevation constant zero point five two
zero
and freezing depression constant one point eight six kelvin kilogram per mole.
An ideal dilute solution shows boiling elevation zero point two six zero
kelvin.
The effective particle molality is therefore zero point five zero zero mole
per
kilogram.
The same particle inventory predicts freezing depression zero point nine three
zero kelvin.
Dividing the two shifts cancels both the formal molality and van't Hoff
factor.
This cancellation does not by itself reveal the solute molar mass or its
dissociation fraction: additional composition information is required.
A mismatch may indicate measurement error, different samples, concentration
dependent association, nonideality or an inappropriate approximation.
The solute must satisfy the conditions of both dilute solution relations,
including negligible volatility for the boiling elevation model.
Treat both shifts as positive magnitudes relative to the pure solvent, and
distinguish a cross check from an independent molecular identification.
Raoult's law can be solved backward from a vapour composition when the liquid
mixture is ideal and both components are volatile.
Suppose the pure component vapour pressures at one temperature are eighty
kilopascals for A and forty for B.
The equilibrium vapour contains A with mole fraction zero point eight zero
zero.
Let x be the liquid mole fraction of A.
Its partial pressure is eighty x, while B contributes forty times one minus x.
Setting eighty x divided by forty plus forty x equal to zero point eight gives
x equal to two thirds.
The total pressure is then sixty six point six seven kilopascals.
The vapour is enriched in the more volatile component A compared with the
liquid.
The vapour sample composition is not the overall composition of an arbitrary
closed two phase sample; a phase fraction balance would also be required for
that question.
The inference assumes equilibrium at the same temperature, an ideal liquid and
approximately ideal vapour behaviour.
Nonideal mixtures require activities or other supplied equilibrium data
instead
of this direct expression.
Vapour composition and the amount removed are separate pieces of information.
Consider an idealized batch balance starting with ten moles of a binary liquid
containing six moles of A and four of B.
Suppose one mole of vapour is removed, with its measured average composition
stated to be eighty mole percent A.
The withdrawn sample therefore contains zero point eight mole A and zero point
two mole B.
The remaining liquid contains five point two moles A and three point eight
moles B, nine moles in total.
Its A mole fraction is five point two divided by nine, about zero point five
seven eight.
Neither the initial fraction zero point six nor the withdrawn vapour fraction
zero point eight describes that residual liquid.
The stated average composition avoids pretending a finite batch withdrawal has
the initial equilibrium vapour composition throughout.
In a real equilibrium distillation the instantaneous vapour composition
changes
as the liquid changes, and a model or measurements are needed to integrate
that
process.
First conserve each component, then form a mole fraction using the correct
final total.
Osmosis can occur between two solutions, not only between pure solvent and a
solution.
Suppose a membrane passes solvent but retains both solutes.
Initially the left compartment has zero point zero one zero mole of a non
electrolyte in one hundred millilitres of solution.
The right has zero point zero two zero mole in the same initial volume.
At the same temperature, the right has twice the ideal dilute osmotic
pressure,
so solvent initially moves from left to right.
For an idealized final state with equal mechanical pressures, additive
solution
volumes and negligible solute volume effects, equal osmotic pressures require
equal final molar concentrations.
The conserved total solute amount is zero point zero three zero mole in zero
point two zero zero litre, giving zero point one five zero molar in each
compartment.
The final left volume is about sixty six point seven millilitres, and the
right
about one hundred thirty three point three.
Thus about thirty three point three millilitres move right.
If a hydrostatic pressure difference builds, concentrations need not become
equal; mechanical pressure can balance the osmotic difference.
A Henry law calculation needs the partial pressure of the particular dissolved
gas, rather than the entire headspace pressure.
State the convention first: gas partial pressure equals the Henry constant
times its dissolved mole fraction.
Suppose an ideal wet gas has total pressure five point zero zero bar.
Its water vapour contributes a supplied zero point zero four zero bar, and A
makes up twenty five percent of the remaining dry gas.
Subtract the water contribution to get four point nine six bar of dry gas.
The partial pressure of A is one quarter of that, one point two four bar.
With the supplied Henry constant twenty thousand bar at that temperature, the
dissolved mole fraction of A is six point two zero times ten to the negative
five.
Using five bar directly would count water and the other gases as though all
were A.
The dry composition convention matters: a mole fraction already defined for
the
complete wet mixture would instead multiply the total pressure directly.
Assume dilute dissolved A, gas ideality and an unchanged temperature and
solvent for this model.
Evaporating solvent changes the denominator of molality even when the
nonvolatile solute amount stays fixed.
Begin with zero point zero one zero zero mole of a non electrolyte in two
hundred grams of water.
Its molality is zero point zero five zero zero mole per kilogram of solvent.
In a supplied model, fifty grams of water are removed while no solute is lost,
and all solute remains dissolved without reaction or association.
The remaining water mass is one hundred fifty grams, or zero point one five
zero kilogram.
The new molality is zero point zero six six seven.
With the water freezing constant one point eight six kelvin kilogram per mole
and van't Hoff factor one, the predicted freezing depression changes from zero
point zero nine three zero to zero point one two four kelvin.
Do not subtract the evaporated mass from the solute amount, and do not treat
total solution mass as solvent mass.
This dilute colligative model describes equilibrium freezing onset after
cooling; it is not a claim that freezing occurs during evaporation.
Precipitation, solute volatility or a changing particle factor would require a
revised balance.
Osmotic pressure can appear as a hydrostatic level difference rather than a
reading in atmospheres.
Consider a membrane that passes solvent but retains the chosen non
electrolyte,
with both free surfaces exposed to the same atmospheric pressure.
In a supplied dilute model with nearly equal constant liquid densities, a
height difference h provides opposing pressure rho g h.
At osmotic equilibrium this balances the osmotic pressure difference.
Let the final measured solution concentration be zero point zero zero two zero
zero mole per litre, with pure solvent on the other side, at three hundred
kelvin.
Convert concentration to two moles per cubic metre before using R eight point
three one four in S I units.
The osmotic pressure is four thousand nine hundred eighty eight point four
pascals.
With density one thousand kilograms per cubic metre and g nine point eight
zero
metres per second squared, the level difference is about zero point five zero
nine metre.
This uses the final concentration: solvent entering during equilibration can
dilute an initially prepared solution.
Unequal column densities, membrane leakage or an external pressure difference
require a revised mechanical and solution balance.
Two gases can dissolve in proportions very different from their proportions in
the surrounding gas.
Use the specified Henry convention: partial pressure equals Henry constant
times dissolved mole fraction.
An ideal gas reservoir has total gas pressure one bar, with eighty percent A
and twenty percent B by mole; any solvent vapour contribution is already
excluded.
At the stated temperature, supplied Henry constants are one thousand bar for A
and one hundred bar for B.
Their partial pressures are zero point eight and zero point two bar.
Dissolved mole fractions in the complete liquid mixture are therefore zero
point zero zero zero eight and zero point zero zero two.
Among the dissolved gas molecules alone, A's fraction is zero point zero zero
zero eight divided by their sum zero point zero zero two eight, or two
sevenths.
Thus B dominates the dissolved gas population even though it was the minority
in the headspace.
In this convention the smaller Henry constant indicates greater solubility at
equal partial pressure.
Assume dilute nonreacting gases, the same solvent and temperature, and a
sufficiently large gas reservoir so dissolution does not change its stipulated
composition.
A measured vapour composition can supply the evidence missing from a total
pressure value alone.
Consider a specified binary liquid at its boiling equilibrium, with liquid
mole
fraction A equal to zero point four zero zero.
At that temperature its measured partial vapour pressures are thirty two and
forty eight kilopascals, so total pressure is eighty.
Dalton's relation gives vapour mole fraction A equal to thirty two divided by
eighty, or zero point four zero zero.
Liquid and vapour compositions match at this nonpure composition: the supplied
equilibrium point is azeotropic.
An equilibrium vaporization stage there gives no composition enrichment.
Now compare the ideal pressure reference at the same temperature, with pure
liquid vapour pressures sixty and fifty kilopascals.
The ideal total is zero point four times sixty plus zero point six times
fifty,
or fifty four kilopascals, below the measured eighty.
This shows positive total deviation as a separate observation.
It is the composition match, not merely that pressure difference, that
establishes the azeotropic point in this dataset.
Do not assume equal component amounts, a fixed molecular compound formula, or
an unchanged azeotropic composition at every pressure.
Partial freezing changes the liquid concentration because the solid need not
carry the solute with it.
In a supplied dilute water model, dissolve eighteen grams of a non electrolyte
of molar mass sixty grams per mole in one kilogram of water.
The solute amount is zero point three zero zero mole.
With freezing constant one point eight six kelvin kilogram per mole, the
initial liquid's freezing onset is depressed by zero point five five eight
kelvin.
Now suppose zero point four zero zero kilogram of pure ice has separated,
while
every solute molecule stays dissolved in the remaining liquid.
Liquid water mass is zero point six zero zero kilogram and liquid molality
rises to zero point five zero zero.
Its equilibrium freezing depression is then zero point nine three zero kelvin.
The original water total still includes the ice, but that ice is not part of
the liquid solvent denominator.
Continuing freezing therefore changes the temperature at which this remaining
liquid can coexist with ice.
The colligative expression alone does not determine heat removal or the amount
of ice formed.
Solute crystallization, solid solution formation, association or strong
nonideality would invalidate the stipulated pure ice and dilute liquid model.
A liquid composition and a vapor composition are different inputs to a phase
equilibrium calculation.
This supporting binary example assumes ideal liquid behavior and ideal vapor
with no other gas; it excludes nonideal mixtures and azeotropes.
At a fixed temperature, component A has a pure vapor pressure of one hundred
kilopascals, while component B has forty kilopascals.
If a liquid has equal mole fractions of the two components, Raoult's law gives
a bubble pressure of seventy kilopascals.
The first vapor bubble is richer in the more volatile component A, with mole
fraction five sevenths.
Now start instead with a vapor having equal mole fractions.
To find the pressure where its first liquid drop appears, write each liquid
